                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man with longstanding history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset numbness. On your neurological exam, you note that he has loss of sensation on the left side of his face, arm, and leg. His motor strength exam is normal, as are his cranial nerves. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his presentation?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Anterior cerebral artery stroke
opb. Middle cerebral artery stroke
opc. Conversion disorder
opd. Thalamic stroke
ope. Basilar artery stroke

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely explanation for the patient's presentation of sudden-onset numbness on the left side of his face, arm, and leg with normal motor strength and cranial nerves is a middle cerebral artery stroke. This is supported by the patient's history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, which increase the risk of stroke. The involvement of the right side of the brain aligns with a cerebral artery stroke, and the focal sensory deficit is suggestive of this etiology. Evidence paths linking hypertensive disease and diabetes mellitus to cerebrovascular accidents further support this conclusion.
